\chapter{Family}
\label{ch:te-family}
\hlchaptermodality{12}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name my parents and my brothers and sisters in Telugu, choosing the right word for older or younger.}

Name \te{నాన్న} and \te{అమ్మ}, then the four age-graded siblings \te{అన్న} · \te{తమ్ముడు} · \te{అక్క} · \te{చెల్లి}, with \te{చెల్లి} being Telugu's own.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[nānna amma anna tammuḍu akka celli]{\te{నాన్న}, \te{అమ్మ}, and four sibling words — Telugu's own twist}

\label{lesson:TE-C12-kutumbam}



\begin{quote}
Telugu also sorts siblings by relative age. Its words for \textquotedblleft{}father\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}younger sister,\textquotedblright{} though, go their own way.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Parents — one matches, one is Telugu's own}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{నాన్న}} (\emph{nānna}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{father}\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{Telugu's own word}, unlike Tamil/ Kannada's \emph{appā/appa}.
  \item \textbf{\te{అమ్మ}} (\emph{amma}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{mother}\textquotedblright{} — matches Tamil/Kannada's \emph{ammā/amma} closely.
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Telugu} & \textbf{meaning} & \textbf{compare Tamil/Kannada} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\te{అన్న}} (\emph{anna}) & \textbf{older} brother & \emph{aṇṇaṉ/aṇṇa} — near match \\
\textbf{\te{తమ్ముడు}} (\emph{tammuḍu}) & \textbf{younger} brother & \emph{tambi/tamma} — near match \\
\textbf{\te{అక్క}} (\emph{akka}) & \textbf{older} sister & \emph{akkā/akka} — near match \\
\textbf{\te{చెల్లి}} (\emph{celli}) & \textbf{younger} sister & \emph{tangai/tangi} — \textbf{Telugu's own word here} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So the \emph{system} — four words, split by relative age rather than just gender — is shared across Tamil, Kannada, and Telugu. But the exact words aren't identical everywhere: Telugu keeps its own \textbf{\te{నాన్న}} for father and \textbf{\te{చెల్లి}} for \textquotedblleft{}younger sister,\textquotedblright{} even while three of the six words line up closely with its cousins.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nānna, amma\textquotedblright{} — father, mother
  \item \textquotedblleft{}anna, tammuḍu\textquotedblright{} — older/younger brother
  \item \textquotedblleft{}akka, celli\textquotedblright{} — older/younger sister — celli is Telugu's own
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two Telugu family words are its own, rather than matching Tamil/Kannada? (\textbf{\te{నాన్న}} \emph{nānna}, \textquotedblleft{}father,\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{\te{చెల్లి}} \emph{celli}, \textquotedblleft{}younger sister.\textquotedblright{}) Does Telugu still split siblings by age the same way? (\textbf{Yes} — the four-way age-before-gender system is shared across the whole Dravidian family, even where the exact words differ.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[da]{\te{ద} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S116-letter-da}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{◌ె} — what does it do? And one from further back: \te{చ}?

One character this time — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{ద}}
\textbf{\te{ద}} — \emph{da}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{d}, it is \textbf{da}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \te{ద} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{ధన్యవాదములు}} \emph{dhanyavādamulu} — thank you (dhanyavādamulu — \textquotedblleft{}utterances of 'worthy'\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\te{లేదు}} \emph{lēdu} — no / there isn't (lēdu)
  \item \textbf{\te{పరవాలేదు}} \emph{paravālēdu} — it's okay / no problem / you're welcome
  \item \textbf{\te{రేపు} \te{కలుద్దాం}} \emph{rēpu kaluddām} — see you tomorrow
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \te{ద} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{ద} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \te{ద} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{ధన్యవాదములు}  ·  \te{లేదు}  ·  \te{నమస్కారం}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{ద} three times, saying \emph{da} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \te{ద} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{ద}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{da}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.

One more, from much earlier: \te{త} — what does it do?
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(dialogue)]{The first three verbs again — one engine, and its negative}

\label{lesson:TE-C12-second-pass-verbs}



\begin{quote}
The first three plain verbs, in any order: \emph{to speak}, \emph{to stay}, \emph{to work}. Say them before reading on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the three verbs, side by side}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{plain verb} & \textbf{the \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} form} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\te{మాట్లాడు}} \emph{māṭlāḍu} — speak & \textbf{\te{మాట్లాడతాను}} \emph{māṭlāḍatānu} \\
\textbf{\te{ఉండు}} \emph{uṇḍu} — be, stay, live & \textbf{\te{ఉంటాను}} \emph{uṇṭānu} \\
\textbf{\te{పని} \te{చేయు}} \emph{pani cēyu} — work & \textbf{\te{పని} \te{చేస్తాను}} \emph{pani cēstānu} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read the right-hand column downwards and listen to the last three sounds of each. \textbf{‑\te{ాను}} every time. Three different verbs, one ending, and it is the ending that means \emph{I}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: stem, then time, then person}]
Every Telugu verb you meet from here is built in that order: the \textbf{stem} says what happens, the next piece says \textbf{when}, the last piece says \textbf{who}. It is the same gluing-on you met on the end of \textbf{\te{ధన్యవాదములు}}, applied to actions rather than nouns.

Because the \emph{who} sits at the end, \textbf{\te{నేను}} is optional — and because the \emph{when} sits in the middle, changing the time never disturbs the person.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — \te{ఉండు} and its negative}]
\textbf{\te{ఉండు}} is the verb of \emph{being there}, and Telugu keeps a dedicated word for its denial: \textbf{\te{లేదు}}, \emph{there is not}. Learn the two as a pair rather than as a verb and a stray word.

That pairing is what makes \textbf{\te{పరవాలేదు}} readable rather than memorised: \emph{paravā} is the bother, \textbf{‑\te{లేదు}} says there is none. A word you took whole when you learned to answer \emph{how are you} turns out to be a sentence built on this verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item I speak Telugu — then drop the pronoun and say it again
  \item where you live, using the \emph{stay} verb
  \item that you work
  \item someone apologises for being late — give the one-word reply
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What ending do all three \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} forms share? (\textbf{‑\te{ాను}}.) In what order does a Telugu verb stack its pieces? (\textbf{Stem, then time, then person}.) Which word denies \textbf{\te{ఉండు}}? (\textbf{\te{లేదు}}.) And what is \textbf{\te{పరవాలేదు}} made of? (\emph{Paravā}, the bother, plus \textbf{‑\te{లేదు}} — there is none.)
\end{tcolorbox}
